title: The Context-Window Safety Degradation Chain: How Long Contexts Dilute Refusal Features

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: mechanistic identification of whether long-context safety degradation is an attention-capacity or positional-encoding problem directly determines whether the fix is architectural or training-based, informing deployment decisions.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Long-context experiments require models with large context windows and significant compute to process long sequences through TransformerLens with hook access. This exceeds beginner CS students' typical setup and 30-hour budget.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: constructing variable-length prompt pairs, measuring refusal direction magnitude as a function of position and length, and disentangling attention entropy vs positional encoding effects requires multiple experimental conditions.

novelty.reasoning: 'When Refusals Fail: Unstable Safety Mechanisms in Long-Context LLM Agents' (arXiv:2512.02445, 2025) directly studies refusal degradation in long-context settings. 'Context Rot' research (Chroma, 2025-2026) establishes attention dilution and lost-in-the-middle effects as core degradation mechanisms. However, these works are primarily behavioral, measuring refusal rate changes and performance drops. The mechanistic question of whether degradation is specifically due to refusal feature dilution in the residual stream (attention-capacity vs positional-encoding) through TransformerLens analysis has not been directly addressed. The behavioral phenomenon is known but the mechanistic interpretability angle adds novelty.
